Processes for Large Loads

3/20/2026


Vistra is filing a courtesy copy of its comments submitted today on Planning Guide Revision Request (PGRR) 145
in the above-referenced Commission control numbers because Vistra’s PGRR145 comments highlight important
interactions between the Proposal for Adoption (PFA) in Project No. 58479, the Proposal for Publication (PFP) in
Project No. 58481, and the proposed Batch Zero timeline and transition criteria that could, as currently proposed,
confound the statutory deadlines for review of Net Metering Arrangements subject to PURA § 39.169. To mitigate
the risk of inequitable impacts and to support compliance with the deadlines in PURA § 39.169(d), Vistra has
proposed that PGRR145 include known Large Loads that will be subject to PURA § 39.169 in the Batch Zero
baseline and continue to evaluate those Large Loads under the “Legacy” Large Load Interconnection Study
process, unless the Large Load opts for evaluation under the Batch process.

Vistra’s PGRR145 comments also note that the proposed requirements for Interconnecting DSP or alternatively
Interconnecting TSP engagement in certain (sometimes critical) steps in the new proposed process may not always
be appropriate or truly required, so recommends greater flexibility for administrative efficiency. This change should
not impact the majority of Large Load interconnections, but helps to ensure all scenarios can work within the
proposed new procedures.

Vistra’s PGRR145 comments also include some very limited feedback on provisions of the Project No. 58481 PFP
that were ported over into PGRR145. Vistra will offer more complete feedback on the Project No. 58481 PFP when
those comments are formally due on April 17, 2026, but includes them here for reference.

Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me at (512) 349-6464.

                                            Comments
  Vistra Operations Company LLC (Vistra) appreciates the opportunity to offer this
  feedback on Planning Guide Revision Request (PGRR) 145 in advance of the March 24,
  2026, Batch Study Process workshop (March 24 Workshop). Vistra’s comments highlight
  and seek to address three main areas of concern: (1) incongruities with the Senate Bill 6
  (SB6) statutory timeline for evaluating system impacts of Large Loads co-located with
  existing generators; (2) adding flexibility to the new references to Interconnecting DSPs
  and Interconnecting TSPs to account for the full diversity of Large Load configurations;
  and (3) Project No. 58481 incorporations that go beyond the appropriate scope of the
  Planning Guide. Additionally, there are a number of miscellaneous issues along with
  suggested clean-ups and clarifications. These comments are layered on top of ERCOT’s
  March 17, 2026 comments. Vistra may file additional comments on PGRR145 on these
  or other issues as necessary.
  Senate Bill 6 Timeline Incompatibility with Batch Zero
  Vistra notes that there are material incompatibilities between the plain text of PURA §
  39.169(d), the Proposal for Adoption (PFA) that the Public Utility Commission of Texas
  (PUCT or Commission) is considering in Project No. 58479, the timelines contemplated
  in the Commission’s Proposal for Publication (PFP) in Project No. 58481 (which is
  embedded, in part, in PGRR145), and the Batch Zero process proposed in PGRR145.
  Put most simply: the Commission’s pending rules would require completion of the Large
  Load interconnection study process and “any other analysis or study that ERCOT
  determines is necessary,” plus significant non-refundable, binding financial and
  contractual commitments to even submit a PURA § 39.169 notice and application. The
  timeline in PGRR145 in combination with those pending rule provisions likely prevents
  the study process from being “complete” until more than nine months after ERCOT has

the information it needs to assess transmission security.1 That is fundamentally
incompatible with the 120-day timeline in PURA § 39.169(d).
However, Net Metering Arrangements between new Large Loads and existing generators
as of September 1, 2025 (39.169 NMAs), are already subject to a defined system impact
analysis process with strict timelines in PURA § 39.169; therefore, a known Large Load
interconnection request with an existing generator that will be deemed a 39.169 NMA
project should be included in ERCOT’s baseline load for Batch Zero and must not be
subjected to delays or re-study in the Batch Zero process, because the proposed Batch
Zero procedural schedule is incompatible with the required SB6 timeline. Furthermore,
Large Loads that are part of 39.169 NMA projects in the future should have the option to
choose between the Legacy Large Load Interconnection process and Batch process.
PURA § 39.169 establishes very clear timelines that apply specifically to 39.169 NMAs
and are fundamentally rooted in the Legislature’s understanding of the Large Load
interconnection process as it existed during the 2025 Texas Legislative Session – that is,
rooted in the TSP-driven serial study process that PGRR145 proposes moving to
Sections 9.9-9.10 as “Legacy” processes (the “batch” terminology and concept did not
enter the ERCOT policy landscape until December 2025, six months after SB6 became
law). Therefore, it is appropriate for 39.169 NMAs to continue to be evaluated through the
Legacy processes (though 39.169 NMAs should also be afforded the option – but not
obligation – to pursue interconnection through the Batch process if they so choose).
PURA § 39.169 specifically requires a notice to be submitted to ERCOT:
          “before implementing a net metering arrangement between an operating facility
          registered with [ERCOT] as a stand-alone generation resource as of September
          1, 2025, and a new large load customer,” with certain limited exclusions.2
          [emphasis added]
This means that the Legislature singled out a specific subset of Large Load customers –
i.e., new Large Load customers establishing a new net metering settlement arrangement
with existing generators – to whom specific additional requirements are applied, including
requirements that ERCOT study the system impacts of the 39.169 NMA and that the
PUCT approve the 39.169 NMA (with or without conditions) prior to implementation. The
policy trade-off embedded in PURA § 39.169 for requiring those additional procedural
steps is that the additional process for those requirements must be streamlined and
strictly limited in timeframe. To that end, PURA § 39.169 also requires that:
          “[ERCOT] study the system impacts of a proposed net metering arrangement and
          removal of generation for which [ERCOT] receives a notice … after [ERCOT]
          receives all information regarding the arrangement required by [ERCOT] to be
          submitted to [ERCOT],” and ERCOT “must complete the study and submit the

expected (by January 29, 2027). Therefore if ERCOT has had submitted to it sufficient information to conduct its transmission
security and resource adequacy analyses prior to August 2026 but Batch Zero were to delay completed studies until June 2027 or
later, a nine month delay is reasonably conceivable consequence – effectively a 75% exceedance of the statutorily-established
deadline.

         results to the commission with any associated recommendations not later than the
         120th day after [ERCOT] receives all required information regarding the
         arrangement.”3 [emphasis added]
Importantly, note that the only reference to completion of a study in PURA § 39.169(d) is
ERCOT’s system impacts study – specifically, that it must be completed within 120 days
of receiving the necessary information to conduct the study. PURA § 39.169(d) could
have said “ERCOT must study the system impacts after it has studied the system impacts
in a Batch study,” but it does not.
Further, PURA § 39.169 requires that within 60 days of receiving ERCOT’s study and
recommendations, the PUCT “shall approve, deny, or impose reasonable conditions on
the proposed net metering arrangement as necessary to maintain system reliability,
including transmission security and resource adequacy impacts.”4 This highlights that a
core function of the 39.169 NMA assessment is reviewing transmission security, and the
Commission’s determination in a 39.169 NMA application will depend materially on
ERCOT’s study. Thus, the timing of ERCOT’s study is an inextricable component of
satisfying the Legislature’s clear 180-day cumulative time clock, which is triggered by the
application, not by ERCOT’s completion of the study.
Simultaneously, the current PFA draft in Project No. 58479 includes in proposed 16 Texas
Admin. Code (TAC) § 25.205 several provisions that would restrain a 39.169 NMA
proceeding from commencing until after the Large Load interconnection study is
“completed.” For instance, proposed 16 TAC 25.205(d)(1)(B) would require that
         “a completed large load interconnection study as the term is defined in the ERCOT
         protocols as of the date the application is filed with the commission or a study
         report from another completed study process to interconnect a large load customer
         that is required by ERCOT protocols as of the date the application is filed with the
         commission.”5
         “Upon confirmation of completion of all studies required by ERCOT under the large
         load interconnection study process, as described in ERCOT protocols, that is in
         effect at the time the application for approval of the net metering arrangement is
         filed with the commission and following receipt of the information described in
         subsection (g)(2) of this section, ERCOT must conduct a study of the system
         impacts of the net metering arrangement, including transmission security and
         resource adequacy impacts, and stranded or underutilized transmission assets
         associated with the net metering arrangement.”6
The Batch Zero process outlined in PGRR145 is plainly intended to address transmission
security, as one of its core purposes is to “[f]acilitate studies to identify potential system
limitations and determine, to the extent feasible, facilities needed to interconnect a new
Large Load to or modify an existing Large Load on the ERCOT network,” specifically that
“[t]he Batch Zero Interconnection Study consists of a singular, system-wide study

covering steady-state analysis and stability screening analysis performed by ERCOT.”
When combined with the extra-statutory “completion” criteria contemplated in the Project
No. 58479 PFA means that a 39.169 NMA would face undue discriminatory treatment
and delays, discouraging the transmission-efficient and timely business development in
Texas and running directly counter to the letter and spirit of SB6. Presuming that the PFA
will not change, it becomes incumbent upon PGRR145 to avoid this outcome – and the
most efficient way to proceed while complying with the statutory timeframe is to continue
to evaluate 39.169 NMAs through the Legacy Large Load Interconnection processes,
while giving the option for 39.169 NMAs to participate in Batch Zero if they so choose.
PGRR145 should grant the widest latitude to 39.169 NMAs in qualifying as base load not
subject to reallocation, while also allowing 39.169 NMAs that choose to participate in
Batch Zero and have had Large Load Interconnection requests submitted on their behalf
to qualify for Batch Zero allocation. That two-pronged approach should help to avoid
unnecessary and discriminatory delays that contemplate inappropriately adding perhaps
more than 9 months to the timeline contemplated by SB6. To support this outcome, Vistra
recommends that 39.169 NMA projects be given greater timing latitude for ERCOT’s
consideration in the Batch Zero baseline, as such projects are much more limited in
number and should have the least marginal impact on ERCOT’s Batch assessment.
Moreover, ensuring that 39.169 NMA projects move expeditiously in accordance with the
statutory 180-day cumulative review period does not compromise transmission grid
reliability concerns. Since a 39.169 NMA project will occur at a generation site whose full
output capacity is handled by an existing transmission point of interconnection, the
transmission security risk is minimal. And the resource adequacy risk is addressed by
backup generation or load curtailment responsibility borne by the load (and outside the
scope of ERCOT’s Large Load interconnection study process). Accordingly, there is little
systemic risk posed by ensuring NMA projects are handled in accordance with the
statutory 180-day cumulative timeline.
In sum, there are both statutory and broader policy alignment issues with timing dynamics
resulting from the sum of the parts in Project Nos. 58479, 58481, and PGRR145 that
would structurally disadvantage 39.169 NMAs relative to other Large Loads. PURA §
39.169 is meant to facilitate co-location of large loads with existing generation resources
as a means of supporting business development in this state – showing Texas is open
for business and supporting the efficient and reliable integration of Large Loads in
ERCOT. There are no more efficient Large Load integration opportunities than co-location
with an existing generator – particularly dispatchable generators. As noted above, they
require less transmission infrastructure and cost to interconnect the Large Load, can free
up other existing transmission infrastructure for other generation resources and loads,
and allow greater and more efficient utilization of existing generation infrastructure
(supporting extended economic life of existing assets while ensuring grid reliability during
system emergencies). Therefore, 39.169 NMAs should be encouraged and not
discouraged or penalized by Texas’ policy framework.
Flexibility to Include Full Diversity of Large Load Configurations
Additionally, Vistra’s comments incorporate changes to allow for flexibility in the
applicability of mandates for intermediate and interconnection agreements with
Interconnecting DSPs and Interconnecting TSPs. There will be circumstances where one

but not both are relevant. For instance, if the Interconnecting DSP has delegated
performance of key interconnection tasks to the Interconnecting TSP (or vice versa), or if
the Interconnecting Large Load Entity (ILLE) will be netted with a co-located generation
resource and not take retail delivery service (e.g., scenarios involving self-service, self-
generators, incidence of tenancy, electric generation equipment lessor or operator, non-
settled generators, etc.), then only an intermediate and interconnection agreement with
the Interconnecting TSP would be required. Furthermore, there are likely situations,
consistent with ERCOT’s contemplated forthcoming development of “export only” BYOG
scenarios, that will include interconnections that never contemplate the load/generation
netted site being a net load consumer. Those situations, like others mentioned above,
would not need a DSP interconnection agreement. Vistra therefore recommends that the
new references to both the “Interconnecting TSP” and/or the “Interconnecting DSP” (and
other areas where ERCOT and/or the Resource Entity may be or should be included)
should all be caveated with “as applicable” to avoid being overly prescriptive and
administratively inefficient.
Limits on Reasonable Scope of Planning Guide vs. Project No. 58481 PFP
Vistra notes that there are several provisions ported over from the Project No. 58481 PFP
that either exceed the reasonable authority of the ERCOT Planning Guide (e.g., requiring
Large Load interconnection fees to offset TSP rate base), exceed the scope of SB6 (e.g.,
certain disclosure requirements), or both. Vistra has not at this time offered specific
redlines for many of these issues and reserves the right to offer supplemental comments
regarding the Project No. 58481 PFP integration. A few select revisions and potential
issues include:
      Clarifying the reference to “property interest” in demonstrating site control to say
       “evidence of” property interest, as the Large Load will not be conveying a property
       interest to the Interconnecting DSP or Interconnecting TSP.
      Reflecting the plain language of SB6 (specifically PURA § 37.0561(d)) to limit the
       scope of potentially duplicative projects to projects “in this state.” While Vistra
       recognizes there is information value to a broader ask, Vistra generally
       recommends avoiding extending beyond the policy established in SB6 unless
       absolutely necessary for SB6 implementation.
      It is beyond the scope of the ERCOT Planning Guide to direct the allocation of
       transmission system costs and/or refund criteria for financial security held by
       Interconnecting TSPs and DSPs
      Cost allocation for purposes of determining the financial security for system
       upgrades is undefined, but that issue is also beyond the scope of the ERCOT
       Planning Guide.

2.1       DEFINITIONS

Load Commissioning Plan (LCP)

An agreed upon schedule between the interconnecting Transmission Service Provider (TSP) and
Interconnecting Large Load Entity (ILLE) for connecting a Large Load in increments defined by
the ILLE, compiled in the format prescribed by ERCOT, detailing dates, cumulative peak
Demand amounts, and transmission upgrades that would be required to be in service for each
amount of peak Demand. The LCP shall cover the time period from the Initial Energization date
up to the final amount of peak Demand.

(2)     The differentiation between these two types of projects is based on whether a
        simultaneously-feasible, security-constrained generating unit commitment and dispatch is
        expected to be available for all hours of the planning horizon that can resolve the system
        reliability issue that the proposed project is intended to resolve. If it is not possible to
        simulate a dispatch of the Generation Resources and ESRs such that all reliability criteria

        simulate a dispatch of the Generation Resources and ESRs in such a way that all
        reliability criteria are met without the project, but the project may allow the reliability
        criteria to be met at a lower total cost, then the project is classified as an economic-driven

        only contingencies and limits that would be considered in the operations horizon shall be
        simulated.

9.1      Introduction

(1)    This Section defines the requirements and processes used to facilitate new or modified
       Large Load interconnections with the ERCOT System. It documents the transition from
       a Legacy process that reliesd on individual Large Load interconnection studies and the
       establishment of to a new process. This process will be referred to as the the Large Load
       Interconnection Study (LLIS) processBatch Zero Process. The Batch Zero Process
       consists of a Batch Zero Interconnection Study and a Batch Zero Refinement Study. The
       requirements are designed to:

       (a)     Facilitate studies to identify potential system limitations and determine, to the
               extent feasible, facilities needed to interconnect a new Large Load to or modify an
               existing Large Load on the ERCOT network;

       (b)     Facilitate orderly and organized Large Load interconnections, while allowing
               ERCOT to determine whether the interconnection of the proposed Large Load
               would comply with North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC)
               Reliability Standards, ERCOT Protocols, ERCOT Planning and Operating
               Guides, Transmission Service Provider (TSP) criteria, and any Applicable Legal
               Authority (ALA);

       (c)     Specify the communications required between Interconnecting Large Load
               Entities (ILLEs), TSPs, Distribution Service Providers (DSPs), Resource Entities,
               Interconnecting Entities (IEs), and ERCOT;

       (d)     Provide the best information on future Large Load additions for use in
               identifying, forecasting, and analyzing short- and long-range ERCOT capabilities,
               demands, and reserves; and

       (e)     Provide ERCOT accurate data about a new and modified Large Load subject to
               the provisions detailed in sSection 9.2.1, Applicability of the Batch ZeroLarge
               Load Interconnection Study Process, a Large Load subject to Section 9.8, Legacy
               Interconnection Study Procedures for Large Loads, and to ensure that ERCOT
               and stakeholders have the information necessary for planning purposes.

(1)     This Section, previously known as Section 9.3, outlines the former procedures for
        conducting a Large Load Interconnection Study (LLIS) for new or modified Large Loads.

9.8.1      Legacy Large Load Interconnection Study (LLIS)

(1)     A LLIS consists of the set of steady-state, stability, short-circuit and other relevant
        studies that are necessary to determine the reliability impact of a Large Load
        interconnection on affected Transmission Facilities and identify the Transmission
        Facilities that are needed to reliably interconnect the new or modified Large Load to the
        ERCOT System.

(2)     If an Interconnecting Entity (IE) or Resource Entity submits a large Generation Resource
        interconnection request, as defined in Section 5.3, Interconnection Study Procedures for
        Large Generators, that also includes a co-located Large Load, the Full Interconnection

        requested Load amount and conform to all study requirements detailed in Sections 5.3
        and 9.3, Interconnection Study Procedures for Large Loads. For any deadlines or
        timelines set out in this section that conflict with the deadlines or timelines in Sections
        5.2, General Provisions, and 5.3, the deadlines or timelines in Sections 5.2 and 5.3 shall

        detailed in Section 9.8.2, Legacy Large Load Interconnection Study Scoping Process.

9.8.3        Legacy Large Load Interconnection Study Description and Methodology

(1)       The primary purpose of the LLIS is to determine whether the amount of Load being
          requested by the ILLE can be placed in service by the desired Initial Energization date
          while maintaining the reliability of the ERCOT System and ensuring compliance with all
          North American Reliability Corporation (NERC) Reliability Standards, Protocols, this
          Planning Guide, and the Operating Guides. The LLIS will also identify any transmission
          improvements needed to serve the full requested Load amount, including individual load
          increments requested by the ILLE in the initial Load Commissioning Plan (LCP).

(2)       The LLIS consists of a series of distinct study elements. The specific elements included
          in a particular LLIS will be stated in the LLIS scope.

(3)       Each proposed Large Load interconnection that requests more than one physical
          transmission interconnection will be studied as an individual study for each
          interconnection to be analyzed separately from all other such requests unless otherwise
          agreed by the TSP(s) in the interconnection study agreement.

(4)       The LLIS process includes developing and analyzing various computer model
          simulations of the existing and proposed ERCOT transmission system. The results from
          these simulations will be utilized by the TSP(s) to determine the impact of the proposed
          interconnection.

(5)       The study shall include an analysis demonstrating the adequate reliability of any
          temporary interconnection configurations.
